title: Boot Verbs and Tener Expressions
bigQuestion: Why do some Spanish verbs change in the middle, and how can you predict where the change happens?

story.title: Cold Rain, Hungry Team
story.kicker: After a muddy game, a soccer team needs food, blankets and the right Spanish verbs.
paragraphs: The rain started in the second half and never stopped. By the final whistle, the Pilsen under-16 team was soaked, muddy and tired. They had lost 2 to 1. Coach Ramírez waved everyone under the bleachers. "¿Tienen frío?" she asked (Are you cold?). Twenty voices answered at once: "¡Sí, tenemos frío!" (Yes, we're cold!).

Marisol wrung out her socks. "Tengo hambre" (I'm hungry), she said. "Y tengo sed" (And I'm thirsty). Her friend Diego laughed. "Siempre tienes hambre" (You're always hungry). Notice that Spanish says she HAS hunger. English says she IS hungry. That small difference trips up almost every new learner.

The coach checked her phone. "¿Quieren tacos o sopa?" (Do you all want tacos or soup?). "¡Queremos sopa!" (We want soup!), the team shouted. The coach said, "Yo pienso que el restaurante cierra a las nueve" (I think the restaurant closes at nine). Querer became quieren and queremos. Pensar became pienso. The middle of each verb kept changing.

At the restaurant, everyone ordered. "Pido el caldo de pollo" (I'm ordering the chicken soup), said Marisol. The server asked, "¿Qué piden ustedes?" (What are you all ordering?). Diego fell asleep on the booth. "Duerme como un bebé" (He sleeps like a baby), someone joked. Pedir became pido. Dormir became duerme.

On the bus home, Marisol listed the verbs in her notebook. Some changed e to ie. Some changed o to ue. Some changed e to i. But nosotros never changed: queremos, pedimos, dormimos. She drew a shape around the forms that changed. It looked like a boot.
story.think: Which verbs in the story changed their middle vowel, and which forms stayed the same as the infinitive?

lessons.title: What a Stem Is
lessons.mainIdea: A verb's stem is what is left after you drop -ar, -er or -ir, and boot verbs change a vowel in that stem.
reading: Picture the coach asking, "¿Quieres sopa?" (Do you want soup?). The verb is *querer* (to want). Drop the -er ending and you have the *stem*: quer-. In regular verbs, the stem never moves. Hablar gives habl-, and every form keeps it: hablo, hablas, habla. You just swap the endings.

Querer is different. Watch it in the present tense: quiero, quieres, quiere, queremos, queréis, quieren. In four forms, the e of quer- turned into ie. The endings are normal -er endings. Only the stem vowel changed. A verb that does this is called a *stem-changing verb*.

Why does this happen? Centuries ago, Latin short vowels that carried the stress split into two sounds in Spanish. So the change appears only where the stress falls on the stem. In queremos, the stress falls on -re-, the ending side, so the stem stays quer-. You do not need the history to use it, but it explains the pattern.

words.d: to want; also to love a person — e→ie: quiero, quieres, quiere, queremos, queréis, quieren
grammar word: the part of a verb left after you drop -ar, -er or -ir (in Spanish, la raíz)
grammar word: a verb whose stem vowel changes in some present-tense forms, also called a boot verb

look.title: Finding the stem
look.text:
hablar → drop -ar → habl-
comer → drop -er → com-
querer → drop -er → quer-
quer- + o → quiero (e became ie)
quer- + emos → queremos (no change)
look.prompt: What is the stem of pensar, and what vowel in it would you expect to change?

check.q: What is the stem of the verb querer?
check.why: Drop the -er ending from querer and quer- is left. Quier- is the changed stem that appears only in some forms.

check.q: Which form of querer completes the sentence? Yo ___ sopa.
check.why: The yo form takes -o, and the stressed stem vowel e becomes ie: quiero.

check.q: Why does queremos NOT change its stem?
choices: Because the stress falls on the ending, not the stem
check.why: The stem changes only when the stress lands on the stem. In que-RE-mos the stress is on the ending side.

lessons.title: Drawing the Boot
lessons.mainIdea: In a stem-changing verb, yo, tú, él/ella/usted and ellos/ustedes change; nosotros and vosotros keep the original stem.
reading: Write the six forms of querer in two columns, the way a conjugation chart looks. Singular on the left: quiero, quieres, quiere. Plural on the right: queremos, queréis, quieren. Now draw a line around every form with ie. The line wraps the whole left column and dips down to catch quieren at the bottom right.

That outline looks like a *boot*, so teachers call these *boot verbs*. The top of the right column, nosotros and vosotros, sits outside the boot. Those two forms keep the infinitive's stem: queremos, queréis. Every stem-changing verb in the present tense follows this same boot shape.

A common mistake is changing every form: "quieremos" instead of queremos. English speakers do this because the change feels like part of the verb. Remember that *nosotros* (we) lives outside the boot. Saying the forms aloud helps. You will hear that the stress in queremos is not on the stem.

words.d: the boot — teachers use it for the shape of stem-changing verb charts
we — in boot verbs this form keeps the original stem: queremos, podemos, pedimos
you all, informal, used mainly in Spain — also outside the boot: queréis, podéis

look.title: The boot on a chart
look.text:
[ quiero  ]   queremos
[ quieres ]   queréis
[ quiere  ]  [ quieren ]
The brackets mark the boot: four forms change e→ie. Queremos and queréis stay outside with the stem quer-.
look.prompt: Draw the same chart for pensar. Which two forms stay outside the boot?

check.q: Which form of querer is OUTSIDE the boot?
check.why: Nosotros (queremos) and vosotros (queréis) sit outside the boot and keep the stem quer-.

check.q: A student writes: Nosotros quieremos pizza. What is wrong?
choices: The nosotros form keeps the stem: queremos
Pizza needs la in front of it
check.why: Nosotros is outside the boot, so the stem stays quer-: queremos.

check.q: Which form of querer goes with ellos?
check.why: Ellos/ellas/ustedes is inside the boot: quier- plus the -er ending -en gives quieren.

lessons.title: Endings Stay Regular
lessons.mainIdea: Boot verbs change only the stem; their endings are the same regular -ar, -er or -ir endings you already know.
reading: Take *cerrar* (to close), an -ar boot verb. The stem is cerr-, and its e becomes ie inside the boot. Now add the normal -ar endings: cierro, cierras, cierra, cerramos, cerráis, cierran. The endings -o, -as, -a, -amos, -áis, -an are exactly the endings of hablar.

That means you already know half of every boot verb. For -er verbs like querer, use -o, -es, -e, -emos, -éis, -en. For -ir verbs like *dormir* (to sleep), use -o, -es, -e, -imos, -ís, -en: duermo, duermes, duerme, dormimos, dormís, duermen. The only new job is the stem.

Here is a safe two-step method. Step one: pick the ending from the subject, as you would for any regular verb. Step two: ask whether the form is inside the boot. If yes, change the stem vowel. If no, leave it. Students who try to memorize every form as a new word get lost. Students who use the two steps do not.

words.d: to close — e→ie: cierro, cierras, cierra, cerramos, cerráis, cierran
to sleep — o→ue: duermo, duermes, duerme, dormimos, dormís, duermen
the ending — the part of a verb that shows the subject (-o, -as, -a…)

look.title: Two steps for cerrar with ellos
look.text:
Step 1 — ending: ellos with an -ar verb → -an.
Step 2 — boot? Ellos is inside the boot → cerr- becomes cierr-.
Result: cierran. "Ellos cierran la puerta." (They close the door.)
look.prompt: Use the two steps to build the nosotros form of cerrar.

check.q: Which form completes the sentence? Tú ___ la ventana. (cerrar)
check.why: Tú takes the -ar ending -as, and tú is inside the boot, so cerr- becomes cierr-: cierras.

check.q: What are the endings of dormir in the present tense?
choices: New endings found only in boot verbs
check.why: Dormir is an -ir verb, so it uses -o, -es, -e, -imos, -ís, -en. Only the stem changes.

check.q: Which form completes the sentence? Nosotros ___ ocho horas. (dormir)
check.why: Nosotros is outside the boot and dormir is an -ir verb: dorm- plus -imos gives dormimos.

lessons.title: E Becomes IE
lessons.mainIdea: Verbs like querer, pensar, empezar and preferir change the stem vowel e to ie inside the boot.
reading: Imagine the team deciding when to leave. "¿A qué hora empieza el partido?" (What time does the game start?). The verb *empezar* (to begin) has the stem empez-. Inside the boot, e becomes ie: empiezo, empiezas, empieza, empezamos, empezáis, empiezan. Say each form aloud as you write it.

*Pensar* (to think) works the same way: pienso, piensas, piensa, pensamos, pensáis, piensan. So do cerrar, entender (to understand) and preferir (to prefer). "Prefiero la sopa" means I prefer the soup. When a verb has two e's, like preferir, only the stressed one changes: pre-FIE-ro.

How do you know which verbs change? You cannot tell from spelling alone. Pensar changes, but llevar (to carry) does not: llevo, not "llievo". Dictionaries and glossaries mark boot verbs with the change in parentheses: pensar (ie). Learn each verb with its label, and the chart builds itself.

words.d: to think — pienso, piensas, piensa, pensamos, pensáis, piensan
to begin or start — empiezo, empiezas, empieza, empezamos, empezáis, empiezan
to prefer — prefiero, prefieres, prefiere, preferimos, preferís, prefieren
to understand — entiendo, entiendes, entiende, entendemos, entendéis, entienden

look.title: Planning after the game
look.text:
Coach: ¿Qué piensan ustedes? (What do you all think?)
Marisol: Pienso que tenemos hambre. (I think we're hungry.)
Diego: Yo prefiero tacos. (I prefer tacos.)
Coach: El restaurante empieza a servir a las seis. (The restaurant starts serving at six.)
look.prompt: Find every e→ie form in the dialogue. Then say what you prefer to eat after a game, using prefiero.

check.q: Which form completes the sentence? La clase ___ a las ocho. (empezar)
check.why: La clase is third person singular, inside the boot: empiez- plus -a gives empieza.

check.q: What does "No entiendo la pregunta" mean?
choices: I don't think about the question.
check.why: Entiendo is the yo form of entender (ie), to understand.

check.q: Which verb does NOT change its stem?
check.why: Llevar is regular: llevo, llevas, lleva. You cannot guess from spelling; boot verbs are marked (ie) in glossaries.

lessons.title: O Becomes UE
lessons.mainIdea: Verbs like poder, dormir, volver and almorzar change the stem vowel o to ue inside the boot.
reading: Back at the bleachers, a player asks, "¿Puedo irme?" (Can I leave?). The verb is *poder* (to be able to, can). The stem pod- turns into pued- inside the boot: puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, podéis, pueden. The same boot, a different vowel pair. Say the forms aloud and listen for the ue.

*Volver* (to return) gives vuelvo, vuelves, vuelve, volvemos, volvéis, vuelven. *Almorzar* (to eat lunch) gives almuerzo, almuerzas, almuerza, almorzamos, almorzáis, almuerzan. Dormir, which you saw earlier, belongs here too. "¿A qué hora vuelves?" means What time are you coming back?

Poder is usually followed by an infinitive, just like can in English: "Puedo jugar" (I can play). Do not conjugate the second verb. A frequent error is "puedo juego", which doubles the conjugation. Only the first verb changes for the subject; the second stays in its -ar, -er or -ir form.

words.d: to be able to, can — puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, podéis, pueden; followed by an infinitive
to return, come back — vuelvo, vuelves, vuelve, volvemos, volvéis, vuelven
to eat lunch — almuerzo, almuerzas, almuerza, almorzamos, almorzáis, almuerzan

look.title: Walking through poder
look.text:
poder → stem pod-
yo: pued- + o = puedo
tú: pued- + es = puedes
ella: pued- + e = puede
nosotros: pod- + emos = podemos (outside the boot)
ellos: pued- + en = pueden
"¿Puedes venir?" (Can you come?)
look.prompt: Build the six forms of volver the same way, and circle the two that keep vol-.

check.q: Which sentence is correct?
check.why: Poder changes o→ue in yo (puedo), and the verb after it stays an infinitive (jugar).

check.q: Which form completes the sentence? Nosotros ___ a casa a las diez. (volver)
check.why: Nosotros is outside the boot, so the stem stays vol-: volvemos. Volvimos is past tense.

check.q: What does "¿Dónde almuerzas?" mean?
check.why: Almuerzas is the tú form of almorzar (ue), to eat lunch.

lessons.title: Jugar: The Only U to UE
lessons.mainIdea: Jugar is the one common verb that changes u to ue: juego, juegas, juega, jugamos, jugáis, juegan.
reading: The team plays soccer, so they need *jugar* (to play a sport or game). Its stem jug- has a u, not an o, yet it follows the o→ue pattern: juego, juegas, juega, jugamos, jugáis, juegan. It is the only everyday verb that does this, so learn it on its own.

Spanish uses jugar a before the name of a sport or game in careful speech: "Juego al fútbol" (I play soccer). Al is a plus el. Many speakers, especially in Latin America, also say "Juego fútbol" without al. Both are used and understood. Just remember that *tocar* (to play an instrument) is a different verb: "Toco la guitarra."

English uses one word, play, for sports and music. Spanish splits them. A common mistake is "Juego el piano", which sounds like you are playing a game with the piano. Use jugar for sports and games, tocar for instruments and music. Say "Juego al fútbol y toco el piano" to practice both.

words.d: to play a sport or game — juego, juegas, juega, jugamos, jugáis, juegan
to play an instrument; also to touch — regular: toco, tocas, toca
soccer — in the U.S., football is el fútbol americano

look.title: Sports or music?
look.text:
Diego juega al fútbol los sábados. (Diego plays soccer on Saturdays.)
Marisol toca la trompeta en la banda. (Marisol plays the trumpet in the band.)
Nosotros jugamos al béisbol en el parque. (We play baseball in the park.)
look.prompt: Write two sentences about yourself: one with juego and one with toco.

check.q: Which form completes the sentence? Ellas ___ al básquetbol. (jugar)
check.why: Ellas is inside the boot: jug- becomes jueg-, plus the -ar ending -an gives juegan.

check.q: How do you say "I play the guitar"?
check.why: Spanish uses tocar for instruments. The yo form is toco.

check.q: Which form of jugar goes with nosotros?
check.why: Nosotros is outside the boot, so the stem stays jug-, with the -ar ending -amos.

lessons.title: E Becomes I
lessons.mainIdea: Some -ir verbs, like pedir, servir and repetir, change the stem vowel e to i inside the boot.
reading: At the restaurant, Marisol says, "Pido el caldo" (I'm ordering the broth). The verb *pedir* (to ask for, order) has the stem ped-. Inside the boot, e becomes i, not ie: pido, pides, pide, pedimos, pedís, piden. This third pattern appears only in -ir verbs.

*Servir* (to serve) gives sirvo, sirves, sirve, servimos, servís, sirven. *Repetir* (to repeat) gives repito, repites, repite, repetimos, repetís, repiten. Your teacher may say "Repitan, por favor" (Repeat, please). You now know where that i comes from.

Pedir and preguntar both translate as ask, but they are not the same. Pedir means to ask FOR something: "Pido agua" (I ask for water). Preguntar means to ask a question: "Pregunto la hora" (I ask the time). Mixing them up is one of the most common errors English speakers make.

words.d: to ask for, to order — pido, pides, pide, pedimos, pedís, piden
to serve — sirvo, sirves, sirve, servimos, servís, sirven
to repeat — repito, repites, repite, repetimos, repetís, repiten
to ask a question — regular -ar verb; not the same as pedir

look.title: At the restaurant
look.text:
Mesero: ¿Qué piden ustedes? (What are you all ordering?)
Diego: Yo pido tacos de pollo. (I'm ordering chicken tacos.)
Marisol: Nosotras pedimos sopa. (We're ordering soup.)
Mesero: Servimos la sopa con tortillas. (We serve the soup with tortillas.)
look.prompt: Find the forms of pedir and servir. Which one is outside the boot, and how can you tell?

check.q: Which form completes the sentence? El mesero ___ la comida. (servir)
check.why: Servir is an e→i verb. El mesero is inside the boot: sirv- plus -e gives sirve.

check.q: How do you say "I ask for help"?
check.why: Asking FOR something uses pedir, which changes e→i: pido.

check.q: Which form completes the sentence? Ustedes ___ la palabra. (repetir)
check.why: Ustedes is inside the boot, and repetir changes e→i: repiten.

lessons.title: Tener: A Boot with a Twist
lessons.mainIdea: Tener is an e→ie verb with an irregular yo form: tengo, tienes, tiene, tenemos, tenéis, tienen.
reading: The coach counts players: "Tengo veinte jugadores" (I have twenty players). *Tener* (to have) is one of the most used verbs in Spanish. It looks like a boot verb: tienes, tiene, tienen change e to ie, and tenemos, tenéis stay outside. You will use it in almost every conversation.

The twist is yo. Instead of "tieno", Spanish says tengo, with a g. A few other verbs share this yo-go pattern, such as venir (to come): vengo, vienes, viene, venimos, venís, vienen. So tener and venir are boot verbs with a special yo form. "Vengo a las seis" means I'm coming at six.

A mistake many learners make is "yo tiengo", mixing the two changes. Keep them separate. Yo gets the g and no ie: tengo. Tú, él, ellos get ie and no g: tienes, tiene, tienen. Nosotros and vosotros get neither: tenemos, tenéis. Practice all six forms until they sound natural.

words.d: to have — tengo, tienes, tiene, tenemos, tenéis, tienen; yo form is irregular
to come — vengo, vienes, viene, venimos, venís, vienen
the player (male / female)

look.title: Three kinds of forms in tener
look.text:
yo → g, no ie → tengo
tú, él, ellos → ie, no g → tienes, tiene, tienen
nosotros, vosotros → neither → tenemos, tenéis
"¿Cuántos hermanos tienes?" "Tengo dos." (How many siblings do you have? I have two.)
look.prompt: Answer in Spanish: ¿Cuántas clases tienes hoy?

check.q: Which form completes the sentence? Yo ___ un perro.
check.why: The yo form of tener is irregular: tengo, with a g and no ie.

check.q: Which form completes the sentence? Mi hermana ___ quince años.
check.why: Mi hermana is third person singular, inside the boot: tiene.

check.q: Which form of venir goes with nosotros?
check.why: Venir is an -ir verb and nosotros is outside the boot: ven- plus -imos gives venimos.

lessons.title: Hungry, Thirsty, Cold, Hot
lessons.mainIdea: Spanish uses tener plus a noun for many feelings English expresses with to be: tengo hambre means I am hungry.
reading: Back in the rain, nobody says "estoy frío". They say "Tengo frío", literally I have cold. Spanish treats hunger, thirst, cold and heat as things you have. *Tener hambre* (to be hungry), *tener sed* (to be thirsty), *tener frío* (to be cold) and tener calor (to be hot).

Because hambre and sed are nouns, you make them stronger with mucho or mucha, not muy. Hambre is feminine, so it is "tengo mucha hambre" (I'm very hungry). Frío and calor are masculine: "tengo mucho frío", "tengo mucho calor". "Tengo muy hambre" is a common learner error; muy goes with adjectives.

Be careful with estar. "Estoy frío" does not mean I feel cold. It sounds like your body is cold to the touch, like food left out. "Estoy caliente" can even have a romantic or embarrassing meaning in many places. To talk about how you feel, use tener.

words.d: to be hungry — literally to have hunger; mucha hambre = very hungry
to be thirsty — literally to have thirst; mucha sed = very thirsty
to be (feel) cold — mucho frío = very cold; opposite of tener calor
to be (feel) hot — mucho calor = very hot

look.title: Under the bleachers
look.text:
Coach: ¿Qué tienen? (What's wrong with you all?)
Marisol: Tengo mucho frío. (I'm very cold.)
Diego: Yo tengo mucha hambre. (I'm very hungry.)
Ana: Y nosotros tenemos sed. (And we're thirsty.)
look.prompt: It is July in Chicago and 95 degrees. Say how you feel with a tener expression and mucho or mucha.

check.q: How do you say "I'm very hungry"?
check.why: Hunger uses tener, and hambre is a feminine noun, so it takes mucha, not muy.

check.q: It is snowing and you are outside without a coat. What do you say?
check.why: To say you feel cold, Spanish uses tener frío. Estoy frío describes something cold to the touch.

check.q: What does "Los jugadores tienen sed" mean?
check.why: Tener sed means to be thirsty.

lessons.title: Fear, Being Right, Luck, Sleep
lessons.mainIdea: Tener miedo, tener razón, tener sueño, tener suerte and tener prisa also use tener where English uses to be.
reading: On the dark bus ride home, Diego whispers, "Tengo miedo de los truenos" (I'm afraid of thunder). *Tener miedo* means to be afraid, and you add de before the thing you fear. The coach nods at Marisol's plan to leave early. "Tienes razón" (You're right). *Tener razón* means to be right.

More of the family: *tener sueño* (to be sleepy), tener suerte (to be lucky), tener prisa (to be in a hurry) and tener cuidado (to be careful). "¡Ten cuidado!" (Be careful!) is something you will hear from any abuela. Each one is tener plus a noun, conjugated for the subject.

Age belongs here too. "Tengo dieciséis años" means I am sixteen, literally I have sixteen years. English speakers often say "soy dieciséis", which sounds like I am the number sixteen. Always use tener with años. "¿Cuántos años tienes?" (How old are you?) is how you ask.

words.d: to be afraid (of) — Tengo miedo de las arañas (I'm afraid of spiders)
to be right — no tener razón = to be wrong
to be sleepy
to be … years old — Tengo quince años (I'm fifteen)

look.title: Which tener expression?
look.text:
You stayed up late studying. → Tengo sueño.
Your bus leaves in two minutes. → Tengo prisa.
You won a raffle. → Tengo suerte.
A dog growls at you. → Tengo miedo.
Your friend says 2 + 2 = 4. → Tienes razón.
look.prompt: Describe two moments from your week using two different tener expressions.

check.q: How do you say "My brother is twelve years old"?
check.why: Age uses tener plus años. Leaving out años or using ser is a common error.

check.q: Your friend gives the correct answer. What do you say?
check.why: To be right is tener razón, so to a friend you say tienes razón.

check.q: What does "Tenemos prisa" mean?
check.why: Tener prisa means to be in a hurry.

review.q: Which form completes the sentence? Nosotros ___ ir al partido. (querer)
review.why: Nosotros is outside the boot, so querer keeps the stem quer- with the -er ending -emos.

review.q: Which form completes the sentence? ¿A qué hora ___ tú? (volver)
review.why: Tú is inside the boot, and volver changes o→ue: vuelves.

review.q: Which verb changes e to i, not e to ie?
review.why: Pedir is an e→i verb (pido, pides). The others change e→ie.
Jugar changes u→ue inside the boot (juega) and is for sports; instruments use tocar.

choices: I have a lot of heat in my house.
review.why: Tener calor means to feel hot; mucho makes it stronger.

review.q: Which form completes the sentence? Yo ___ tres hermanos. (tener)
review.why: Tener has an irregular yo form: tengo.

review.q: A student says "Yo puedo juego". What should it be?
review.why: Only poder is conjugated (puedo); the second verb stays an infinitive (jugar).

review.q: In the story, why does Marisol draw a boot around the verb forms?
choices: Because the team plays soccer in boots
Because only the nosotros forms changed
Because the forms that change make a boot shape on the chart
review.why: Yo, tú, él and ellos change the stem; outlined on a chart they form a boot, with nosotros and vosotros outside.
